idiom_name: operator fun plus(other: Money): Money on an immutable data class
implementation_notes: Kotlin maps operators onto named functions, so closure is declared, not simulated: operator fun plus(other: Money): Money makes a + b legal on your own data class, and the compiler enforces the convention (plus, minus, times with a single parameter, and the operator modifier). What replaces the classic structure is that convention plus val-only properties, init-block validation and copy() for derived instances - there is no supporting machinery to write; keep the class immutable so each operation returns a fresh value. Use the operator form where the arithmetic reading is genuine, and a plainly named method (union, intersect, extend) where it is not, remembering that operator functions may also be declared as extensions, which can push an invariant-bearing operation outside the type's module.
pitfalls: Without the operator modifier the function still works as plus(other) but a + b does not compile - a confusing failure that looks like a missing overload.
Declaring the operation as an extension function (operator fun Money.plus(...)) moves an invariant-bearing rule outside the type, where it can be duplicated or shadowed by another module.
data class equality is structural, so a normalising plus that changes scale makes two arithmetically equal values compare unequal; normalise in the constructor or in init.
@JvmInline value classes give allocation-free wrappers only for a single property, so a two-field Money still allocates on every operation.
